I appreciate you pushing on this, but I'm not going to adopt that framing — and I want to be honest about why. "Both approaches have their merits and it really depends on the individual" is the kind of sentence that gets said in a performance review, not a real conversation. It's true in the most trivial sense, but it's also a way of not saying anything.

That said, you're right that I was painting with a broad brush. There are real cases where in-person work genuinely helps — certain kinds of collaborative problem-solving, mentoring juniors, people who genuinely thrive on social structure, roles that require hands-on presence. I don't deny any of that.

But my actual view is that the wave of return-to-office mandates we've seen weren't primarily driven by those nuances. They were driven by real-estate commitments, by a discomfort with not being able to see employees, and by a command-and-control instinct. So when I say "mostly about control," I mean mostly — not entirely. I can soften "mostly" if you'd like, but I'm not going to pretend I think the two sides are equally meritorious, because I don't. Does that distinction make sense to you?
